result.abstract: The lecture describes the brainstem, the stalk connecting the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum, made of the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata, with its embryological origin, connections and external and internal configuration. It dwells on where each cranial nerve emerges, on the fourth ventricle, the reticular formation and the running tracts, and on the fact that the brainstem runs vital functions. It ends with the blood supply from the basilar artery and the alternating syndrome that locates a lesion to a level of the brainstem.

concepts.name: Brainstem
concepts.definition: The stalk connecting the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum, made of the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata from above downwards. It lies in the posterior cranial fossa and is responsible for vital functions such as breathing, consciousness, blood pressure, heart rate and sleep.

evidence.quote: The brainstem connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum
Brainstem: midbrain, pons, medulla, in the posterior cranial fossa on the clivus
It is composed of 3 sections in descending order: the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata

concepts.name: Midbrain
concepts.definition: The uppermost and smallest part of the brainstem, about 2 cm long, which passes through the tentorial opening. It has two parts: the tectum behind the cerebral aqueduct and the paired cerebral peduncles anterolaterally.

evidence.quote: The smallest part, about 2 cm, passing through the tentorial opening (foramen of Pacchioni)
The midbrain is the smallest of the three regions of the brainstem, measuring around 2cm in length
Midbrain: smallest, 2 cm; tectum with four colliculi; peduncles with CN III between them

concepts.name: Pons
concepts.definition: The middle and largest part of the brainstem, derived from the metencephalon with the cerebellum. Its ventral bulge, about 2.5 cm, is made by transverse pontocerebellar fibres, and CN V to VIII are associated with it.

evidence.quote: The largest part, from the metencephalon with the cerebellum
Pons: largest; basilar artery in the basilar groove; CN V to VIII
The anterior or ventral surface of the pons is marked by a bulging formed by the transverse pontocerebellar fibres

concepts.name: Medulla oblongata
concepts.definition: The lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord, bearing the pyramids and olives on its ventral surface. Four cranial nerves emerge from it and it holds the respiratory and cardiovascular centres.

evidence.quote: Medulla: pyramids (corticospinal), olives (inferior olivary nucleus)
the respiratory and cardiovascular centres are in the medulla
Nerves emerging from Medulla (4 nerves)

concepts.name: Inferior quadrigeminal brachium
concepts.definition: The brachium that conveys fibres from the lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body, for hearing.

concepts.definition: One of the paired thick pillars on the anterolateral midbrain, extending from the cerebral hemispheres to converge at the pons and carrying descending fibres; the two are separated by the interpeduncular fossa.

concepts.name: Oculomotor nerve

concepts.name: Trochlear nerve

concepts.name: Facial nerve

concepts.name: Intermediate nerve

concepts.definition: The second cranial nerve, running from the eye to the optic chiasm; one of the two cranial nerves that do not arise from the brainstem.

concepts.name: Olfactory nerve
concepts.definition: The first cranial nerve; one of the two cranial nerves that do not arise from the brainstem.

evidence.quote: with the exception of two: the optic nerve and the olfactory nerve

concepts.name: Cranial nerve nucleus
aliases: nuclei of origin of cranial nerves
concepts.definition: Grey matter of the brainstem from which a cranial nerve arises; ten of the twelve cranial nerves arise from their nuclei in the brainstem.

evidence.quote: Ten of the twelve cranial nerves arise from their cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem
grey matter (the cranial nerve nuclei and the reticular formation)

concepts.name: Basilar groove
concepts.definition: The groove marking the midline of the ventral surface of the pons, in which the basilar artery lies.

concepts.name: Basilar artery
concepts.definition: The artery lying in the basilar groove of the pons which, with its branches, supplies the brainstem. Its branches include the posterior cerebral artery and its peduncular branch, the superior cerebellar artery, the posterior choroidal artery and the interpeduncular branches.

evidence.quote: The brainstem receives vascular supply from the basilar artery and its branches

concepts.name: Pontomedullary junction
concepts.definition: The angle between the lower border of the pons and the superior border of the medulla, an important landmark where CN VI, VII and VIII emerge from medial to lateral.

evidence.quote: The pontomedullary junction is an important anatomical landmark defined by the angle between the lower border of the pons and the superior border of the medulla
VI, VII, VIII at the pontomedullary junction (medial to lateral)

concepts.name: Cerebellopontine angle
concepts.definition: The angle formed at the junction of the pons, medulla and cerebellum, where the cerebellar flocculus, the choroid plexus and the emerging CN VII and VIII surround the foramen of Luschka.

evidence.quote: The angle formed at the junction of the pons, medulla, and cerebellum is another anatomical landmark and is named cerebellopontine angle
Cerebellopontine angle: CN VII and VIII beside the foramen of Luschka

concepts.name: Foramen of Luschka
aliases: lateral aperture of the fourth ventricle
concepts.definition: One of the two lateral apertures of the fourth ventricle, by which CSF leaves it; it lies at the cerebellopontine angle beside the emerging CN VII and VIII.

CSF leaves by the median foramen of Magendie and two lateral foramina of Luschka

concepts.name: Foramen of Magendie
concepts.definition: The single median foramen of the fourth ventricle, by which CSF leaves it.

evidence.quote: CSF leaves by the median foramen of Magendie and two lateral foramina of Luschka
CSF exits via Magendie (median) and Luschka (lateral)

concepts.name: Fourth ventricle
concepts.definition: The ependymal cavity lying behind the pons and medulla. Its roof is the superior and inferior medullary vela, its floor the rhomboid fossa and its side walls the vela and cerebellar peduncles; CSF leaves it by the foramen of Magendie and the two foramina of Luschka.

evidence.quote: Roof: the superior and inferior medullary vela. Floor: the rhomboid fossa. Side walls: the vela and cerebellar peduncles

concepts.name: Rhomboid fossa
concepts.definition: The diamond-shaped depression on the dorsal surface of the pons and upper half of the medulla that forms the floor of the fourth ventricle.

concepts.name: Fastigium

concepts.name: Facial colliculus
concepts.definition: A bulge in the floor of the fourth ventricle formed by fibres of the facial nerve looping around the abducens nucleus; a lesion there gives an ipsilateral VI and VII palsy.

evidence.quote: The facial colliculus is a bulging formed by the fibres of the facial nerve looping around the abducens nucleus

concepts.name: Ventral median fissure

concepts.name: Pyramid of the medulla
concepts.definition: An elevation on either side of the ventral median fissure of the medulla, produced by the corticospinal tract.

concepts.name: Olive

concepts.name: Inferior olivary nucleus
concepts.definition: The nucleus that produces the olive of the medulla; it is important in the control of movement.

concepts.name: Pyramidal decussation
concepts.definition: The crossing of most corticospinal fibres, 75 to 90 percent, in the lower medulla, marking the lower part of the ventral median fissure.

the pyramids decussate in the medulla

concepts.name: Corticospinal tract
concepts.definition: A descending motor tract which, with the corticobulbar tract, forms the motor pathway for voluntary movement of the body and face. It produces the pyramid of the medulla, and 75 to 90 percent of its fibres cross in the lower medulla.

evidence.quote: Corticospinal and corticobulbar | Descending | Voluntary movement of body and face
the motor pathway, which is composed by the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts

concepts.name: Corticobulbar tract
concepts.definition: A descending tract which, with the corticospinal tract, forms the motor pathway controlling voluntary skeletal muscle activity of the body and face.

evidence.quote: composed by the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts. It controls the voluntary skeletal muscle activity of the body and face

concepts.name: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway
concepts.definition: An ascending conscious tract through the brainstem carrying touch, proprioception and vibration.

evidence.quote: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus | Ascending, conscious | Touch, proprioception, vibration

concepts.name: Anterolateral system
concepts.definition: An ascending conscious tract through the brainstem, also called spinothalamic, carrying crude touch, pain and temperature.

evidence.quote: Anterolateral (spinothalamic) | Ascending, conscious | Crude touch, pain, temperature
Conscious tracts : comprised of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway and the anterolateral system

concepts.name: Spinocerebellar tract
concepts.definition: An ascending unconscious tract through the brainstem carrying proprioception to the cerebellum.

evidence.quote: Spinocerebellar | Ascending, unconscious | Proprioception to the cerebellum

concepts.name: Reticular formation
concepts.definition: A network of neuronal cell bodies and small axon bundles running in many directions, without distinct boundaries, spread from the spinal cord through the brainstem to the hypothalamus and thalamus. It integrates vital functions: arousal, consciousness, sleep-wake cycles, motor coordination, cardiovascular and respiratory control, pain modulation and habituation.

evidence.quote: It integrates vital functions: arousal, consciousness, sleep-wake cycles, motor coordination, cardiovascular and respiratory control, pain modulation and habituation
The reticular formation (RF) consists of an intricate mixture of neuronal cell bodies and fascicles of axons running in small bundles
Reticular formation: consciousness, sleep, breathing, heart rate, pain

concepts.name: Respiratory and cardiovascular centres
concepts.definition: The centres for breathing and cardiovascular control, located in the medulla oblongata, which is why compression or a lesion of the medulla is life-threatening.

evidence.quote: the respiratory and cardiovascular centres are in the medulla
cardiovascular and respiratory centres (medulla)
The respiratory and cardiovascular centres are in the medulla, which is why medullary compression is life-threatening

concepts.name: Alternating syndrome
concepts.definition: The association of a peripheral cranial nerve palsy on one side with a hemiplegia on the opposite side. It locates the lesion to a level in the brainstem, the cranial nerve involved indicating the level.

evidence.quote: A peripheral cranial nerve lesion on one side with a hemiplegia on the other locates the lesion to a level in the brainstem

The association of the peripheral involvement of a cranial nerve with a hemiplegia realizes an alternating syndrome

concepts.name: Hemiplegia
concepts.definition: Weakness of the arm and leg on one side of the body; in an alternating syndrome it lies on the side opposite the cranial nerve palsy.

evidence.quote: ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy plus contralateral hemiplegia

concepts.name: Acoustic neuroma

evidence.quote: an acoustic neuroma gives unilateral deafness, tinnitus, then facial and trigeminal signs

notes: The packet contains no known-concept list, so all concept names are my own standard English forms.

The concept count (71) is above the typical range because the lecture names ten cranial nerves, each with its own emergence landmark, plus many surface and ventricular landmarks that are tested individually.

Cranial nerve emergence has no dedicated relation type. I used branch-of (read as 'arises from') for a nerve emerging from a part of the brainstem, located-in for a nerve emerging at a named landmark (interpeduncular fossa, pontomedullary junction, cerebellopontine angle), and related-to for emergence in front of or behind the olive or pyramid.

'Bulbopontine groove' (summary table and slide 20) is given as an alias of 'Pontomedullary junction' because the packet lists the same nerves (VI, VII, VIII, medial to lateral) at both; the packet never states the equivalence outright.

hy:1 writes 'Midbrain (mesencephalon, smallest)' as if mesencephalon were a synonym of midbrain; I kept Mesencephalon, Metencephalon and Myelencephalon as separate concepts for the embryonic vesicles, as the embryology table and questions treat them.
q:zdor62 calls the midline landmark of the fourth ventricle floor the 'median eminence' while the summary and slide 15 say 'medial eminence'; recorded as an alias.

Slide 20 uses older nerve names from OCR text: 'common occulomotor nerve' (III), 'external oculomotor' (VI), 'pathetic nerve' (IV), 'cochleo-vestibular' (VIII) and 'the spinal nerve' (XI); slide 17 instead speaks of the 'cranial part of accessory'. These are recorded as aliases.
Slide 3 and slide 5 say 'posterior cerebral fossa' / 'cerebral posterior fossa' where the summary says 'posterior cranial fossa'; recorded as aliases.

Acoustic neuroma: hy:9 names it and deeper:4 describes 'a tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve sheath' at the same site without using the name; the link between the two is inferred, hence medium confidence.

Branches of the basilar artery (posterior cerebral, superior cerebellar, posterior choroidal, interpeduncular) and the medullary vela are only listed in the packet, so they are kept inside the definitions of Basilar artery and Fourth ventricle rather than made into separate concepts.

findings.detail: The packet supports the definition, but standard embryology calls the bend between brainstem and spinal cord the cervical flexure; the cephalic flexure is the mesencephalic flexure itself. In standard teaching this concept and 'mesencephalic-flexure' are therefore one and the same thing, not two bends (the result records this under conflicts but still keeps two concepts).

evidence.quote: the cephalic flexure: brainstem and spinal cord
The growing neural tube bends at the cephalic flexure and the mesencephalic (cranial) flexure

findings.detail: The packet says the medial eminence marks the midline, but in standard teaching the midline of the floor of the fourth ventricle is the median sulcus; the medial eminence is the paired longitudinal elevation on each side of it (the facial colliculus is its lower part). The alias 'median eminence', taken from a question option, is in standard usage a hypothalamic structure, not this landmark.

findings.detail: The definition calls the accessory nerve 'one of the mixed nerves', which the packet supports (the French grouping of IX, X and XI), but standard teaching is that CN XI is a purely motor nerve; only IX and X are mixed. The alias 'spinal nerve' is the slide's literal rendering of the French name for CN XI and in English means a nerve of the spinal cord, so it is misleading as a search alias.

evidence.quote: Lateral, behind the olive | IX, X and XI, the mixed nerves

findings.detail: The definition says the basilar artery and its branches supply the brainstem, as the slide does, but standard teaching is the vertebrobasilar system: the medulla is supplied mainly by the vertebral arteries and their branches, which the packet itself hints at and the definition leaves out. The posterior choroidal artery is also normally taught as a branch of the posterior cerebral artery, not of the basilar artery directly.

evidence.quote: The brainstem receives vascular supply from the basilar artery and its branches
Blood supply = basilar (+ vertebral) system

findings.detail: Read as a sentence, 'Oculomotor nerve is a branch of Midbrain' is not what the packet says: it says the nerve emerges from (exits) the surface of the midbrain, and branch-of is meant for a nerve or vessel arising from a parent nerve or vessel. The same applies to the other seven branch-of relations (trochlear-nerve to midbrain; trigeminal-nerve and abducens-nerve to pons; hypoglossal-, glossopharyngeal-, vagus- and accessory-nerve to medulla-oblongata); related-to, or located-in as used for the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves, would not misstate the link.
